briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Doors Open, Cases Move: Michigan Operators Find Footing as National Rescheduling and Psychedelics Momentum Builds
briefs.top: Michigan operators are notching real wins this week — new store openings, a surveillance-camera fight won, and a bipartisan push to unwind the 24% wholesale tax — even as the state's cannabis market keeps adjusting to that levy. Nationally, the mood is bullish: DEA's Schedule III hearing process is grinding forward, Congress just bought the hemp industry a reprieve, and psychedelics keep racking up FDA fast-track wins.

local.text: Lume Cannabis Co. opened its new Ann Arbor location at 2247 W. Liberty Street with a three-day grand opening running 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. — fresh retail footprint landing right in Sticky Trap's backyard.

Upper Peninsula chain Rize, which operates three U.P. locations, is bucking the tax-driven contraction other operators face by negotiating cost-sharing deals with suppliers to split the wholesale tax burden instead of eating it alone.

Jars Cannabis notched a regulatory win in Madison Heights, getting the parking-lot-facing Flock surveillance camera taken down after pushing back on a 2022 settlement requirement — a small but real precedent for operators negotiating with skeptical municipalities.

Muskegon's Fields Cannary is pushing dispensary format further than most Michigan operators have gone, targeting a fall opening for its retail cannabis shop with a full-service restaurant to follow — a hospitality-forward bet even in a tightening market.

Relief may be coming on the tax fight: Treasury data show the 24% wholesale tax has collected less than $34 million in its first four months — a third of projections — fueling a new GOP repeal bill (HB 6224) and a gubernatorial candidate's pledge to roll back the levy.

national.text: DEA's marijuana rescheduling hearing is actively underway after Acting AG Blanche's order immediately placed FDA-approved and state medical marijuana products into Schedule III, with the broader Schedule I-to-III hearing running through mid-July at DEA headquarters.

FDA handed three companies — Compass Pathways, Usona Institute and Transcend Therapeutics — National Priority Vouchers that compress psychedelic drug reviews for depression and PTSD treatments down to 1-2 months, a major acceleration for psilocybin and MDMA-adjacent therapies.

Compass Pathways locked in the final piece of its approval case, posting positive 26-week durability data from its COMP006 trial in July, putting COMP360 psilocybin on track to become the first classic psychedelic cleared in the U.S.

The U.S. House voted 370-48 on Sept. 1 to accept the Senate's delay of the federal hemp THC ban, pushing the restrictive new definition from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11 and buying the $28 billion hemp industry another month to lobby for a workable regulatory framework.

Not every signal is smooth sailing: DEA is sending Colorado medical cannabis businesses a 26-question compliance questionnaire — including whether they source product from other states — before granting the federal protections tied to rescheduling, a reminder that the path to Schedule III still comes with real paperwork.
